meta.titre: Apparatus and experiments: measuring, separating, collecting gases and safety

sections.contenu_markdown: In a school laboratory in Bafoussam, a student must separate sand from salty water, collect a gas without losing it into the room, and measure 25.0 cm$^3$ of a solution accurately. Each task needs a different piece of apparatus, and a wrong choice costs marks in the practical paper and in the written paper. Questions on apparatus and experiments are among the most common in the GCE O/L Chemistry paper because they test whether you have really worked in the laboratory. This course shows how to choose the right apparatus, method and safety step.

items: Volume is measured in cm$^3$ or dm$^3$, and 1 dm$^3$ = 1000 cm$^3$.
A mixture contains substances that are not chemically joined.
A solute dissolves in a solvent to make a solution.
A gas can be lighter or denser than air.

sections.titre: Choosing laboratory apparatus and working safely
sections.contenu_markdown:
Choose the apparatus by asking **what must be measured or done, and how accurately**.

| Apparatus | Use |
|---|---|
| Beaker | Holding, mixing or heating liquids (volume only approximate) |
| Conical flask | Holding the solution being titrated; it can be swirled without spilling |
| Measuring cylinder | Measuring a volume of liquid roughly |
| **Pipette** (with a filler) | Measuring **one fixed volume accurately**, for example 25.0 cm$^3$ |
| **Burette** | Delivering **any volume accurately**, drop by drop, in a titration |
| Volumetric flask | Making a solution of exact volume |
| Gas syringe | Measuring the volume of a gas given off |
| Thermometer, stopwatch, balance | Measuring temperature, time and mass |
| Filter funnel and filter paper | Filtration |
| Evaporating dish | Evaporating a solution |
| Bunsen burner, tripod and gauze | Heating |
| Liebig condenser | Cooling a vapour to a liquid in distillation |
| Separating funnel | Separating liquids that do not mix |

**Safety rules.** Wear safety goggles and a lab coat, tie back long hair, and never taste chemicals. Read the hazard symbol on a bottle (corrosive, flammable, toxic, irritant). Do not heat flammable liquids such as ethanol with a naked flame; use a hot water bath. Use a **fume cupboard** for poisonous gases such as chlorine, sulphur dioxide and nitrogen dioxide. When diluting, add **acid to water**. Point a heated test tube away from people, and report spills and breakages at once.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a mixture is described and the method must be chosen
variantes.contenu_markdown:
| Mixture | Method | Why it works |
|---|---|---|
| Insoluble solid and liquid (sand and water) | **Filtration** | The solid stays on the filter paper |
| Soluble solid from a solution (salt from salt solution) | **Evaporation**, or **crystallisation** for crystals | The water leaves and the solid remains |
| Pure solvent from a solution (water from salty water) | **Simple distillation** | The solvent boils, the vapour is condensed, and the solute stays behind |
| Two liquids that mix, with different boiling points (ethanol and water) | **Fractional distillation** | The liquid with the lower boiling point distils first |
| Two liquids that do not mix (oil and water) | **Separating funnel** | The lower layer is run off |
| Dyes in an ink | **Paper chromatography** | Different dyes travel at different speeds up the paper |
| Iron filings and sulphur | **Magnet** | Only iron is attracted |
| Ammonium chloride and sand | **Sublimation** (heating) | Ammonium chloride changes to gas and then back to solid |

In a Liebig condenser the cooling water enters at the **bottom** and leaves at the **top**, so that the jacket stays full.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a gas is prepared and the question asks how to collect or test it
variantes.contenu_markdown:
| Gas | Preparation | Collection | Test |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hydrogen | Zinc with dilute acid | Over water, or upward delivery | Lighted splint gives a squeaky pop |
| Oxygen | Hydrogen peroxide with manganese(IV) oxide | Over water | Relights a glowing splint |
| Carbon dioxide | Marble chips with dilute hydrochloric acid | Downward delivery (denser than air) | Limewater turns milky |
| Ammonia | Heating an ammonium salt with calcium hydroxide | **Upward delivery** | Turns damp red litmus blue |
| Chlorine | Concentrated hydrochloric acid with an oxidising agent | Downward delivery, in a fume cupboard | Bleaches damp litmus paper |
| Sulphur dioxide | Acid with a sulphite | Downward delivery, in a fume cupboard | Turns acidified potassium dichromate(VI) from orange to green |

A gas **denser than air** is collected by **downward delivery** and a gas **lighter than air** by **upward delivery**. A gas that is not very soluble can be collected **over water**, and its volume can be measured in a gas syringe. Gases are dried with concentrated sulphuric acid, except ammonia, which is dried with calcium oxide.

$\mathrm{Zn + 2HCl \rightarrow ZnCl_{2} + H_{2}}$

$\mathrm{2H_{2}O_{2} \rightarrow 2H_{2}O + O_{2}}$

variantes.quand_utiliser: When results are tabulated or a graph must be plotted
variantes.contenu_markdown:
To follow a reaction that gives a gas, measure the **gas volume at regular times**. Put the quantity you control (time) on the **x-axis** and the measured quantity (volume) on the **y-axis**. Label both axes with the quantity and unit, choose a scale that uses more than half the grid, plot points with small crosses, and draw a **smooth curve of best fit**.

Average rate $= \dfrac{\text{change in volume}}{\text{change in time}}$. The curve is **steepest at the start**, when the reactants are most concentrated, and becomes **flat** when one reactant is used up.

The rate increases with higher concentration, higher temperature, smaller particle size (powder instead of lumps) and a suitable catalyst.

sections.enonce_markdown:
A student adds a piece of magnesium ribbon to excess dilute hydrochloric acid and collects the gas in a gas syringe. The volumes of gas are recorded every 20 s.

| Time / s | 0 | 20 | 40 | 60 | 80 | 100 | 120 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Volume of hydrogen / cm$^3$ | 0 | 15 | 27 | 37 | 44 | 48 | 48 |

(a) Write the equation. (b) Calculate the average rate from 0 to 20 s, from 40 to 60 s and from 80 to 100 s. (c) Explain the change in rate. (d) Explain why the volume stops at 48 cm$^3$ and use it to find the mass of magnesium used. ($A_r$: Mg = 24; 1 mole of gas = 24 000 cm$^3$.)

etapes.justification: A metal reacts with an acid to give a salt and hydrogen.

etapes.action: Calculate the average rate in each interval.
etapes.justification: Rate = change in volume divided by change in time.
As the acid is used up, the particles of acid collide with the magnesium less often.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The rate **decreases** as the reaction goes on because the concentration of the acid and the amount of magnesium fall.

etapes.action: Explain why the volume stops at 48 cm$^3$.
etapes.justification: The acid is in excess, so the magnesium is the reactant that runs out.
etapes.resultat_markdown: After about 100 s all the magnesium has reacted, so no more gas forms.

etapes.justification: Use the volume of hydrogen and the 1 : 1 ratio.

sections.conclusion_markdown: The rate falls from **0.75** to **0.50** to **0.20 cm$^3$/s** because the reactants are being used up, and the magnesium used had a mass of **0.048 g**.

items.erreur_markdown: A measuring cylinder is as good as a pipette for measuring 25.0 cm$^3$ of a solution in a titration.
items.pourquoi_faux: A measuring cylinder is only approximate. A pipette delivers one fixed volume with high accuracy.
items.correction_markdown: Use a **pipette** for the fixed volume and a **burette** for the volume that is varied.

items.erreur_markdown: Ammonia is collected by downward delivery and dried with concentrated sulphuric acid.
items.pourquoi_faux: Ammonia is lighter than air and very soluble in water, so it is collected by upward delivery. It reacts with sulphuric acid, so that drying agent cannot be used.
items.correction_markdown: Collect by **upward delivery** and dry with **calcium oxide**.

items.erreur_markdown: The cooling water enters at the top of the condenser and leaves at the bottom.
items.pourquoi_faux: Water entering at the top drains straight out and the jacket is not full, so cooling is poor.
items.correction_markdown: Water enters at the **bottom** and leaves at the **top**.

items.erreur_markdown: Salt can be obtained from salt solution by filtration.
items.pourquoi_faux: Dissolved salt passes through the filter paper. Filtration only removes undissolved solids.

items.erreur_markdown: On a graph, join the points with straight lines from point to point, and put the volume on the x-axis.
items.pourquoi_faux: Experimental points have small errors, so a smooth curve of best fit is used. Time is the quantity you control, so it goes on the x-axis.
items.correction_markdown: Time on the x-axis, volume on the y-axis, and a **smooth curve**.

items.enonce_markdown: Name the piece of apparatus that is used (a) to measure exactly 25.0 cm$^3$ of a solution, (b) to add acid drop by drop in a titration, (c) to measure the volume of a gas given off, (d) to separate oil from water.
A mixture contains iron filings, sand and common salt. Describe how you would obtain a sample of each of the three solids.
items.solution_markdown: Move a **magnet** over the dry mixture to remove the **iron filings**. Add the rest to water and stir so that the salt dissolves. **Filter** the mixture: the **sand** stays on the filter paper, and it is washed with distilled water and dried. Heat the filtrate in an **evaporating dish** (or leave to crystallise) until the **salt** remains.

items.enonce_markdown: Ammonia is prepared by heating a mixture of ammonium chloride and calcium hydroxide in a test tube. ($A_r$: N = 14; H = 1; Cl = 35.5; 1 mole of gas = 24 dm$^3$.) (a) Write the balanced equation. (b) Say why the test tube is held with its mouth slightly lower than its base. (c) Describe how the gas is dried, collected and tested. (d) Calculate the maximum volume of ammonia from 5.35 g of ammonium chloride.
items.solution_markdown: (a) $\mathrm{2NH_{4}Cl + Ca(OH)_{2} \rightarrow CaCl_{2} + 2NH_{3} + 2H_{2}O}$ (b) The water that forms condenses at the cool mouth of the tube. If the mouth were higher, the water would run back onto the hot glass and crack it. (c) The gas passes through a tube of **calcium oxide** to dry it. Ammonia is lighter than air, so it is collected by **upward delivery** in an inverted gas jar. It is tested with **damp red litmus paper**, which turns **blue**. (d) $M_r(\mathrm{NH_4Cl}) = 14 + 4 + 35.5 = 53.5$, so $n = 5.35 / 53.5 = 0.10$ mol. The ratio is 2 : 2, so $n(\mathrm{NH_3}) = 0.10$ mol and $V = 0.10 \times 24 = $ **2.4 dm$^3$**.

items_markdown: Use a **pipette** for one fixed volume, a **burette** for variable volumes, a **gas syringe** for gas volumes, and a measuring cylinder only for rough volumes.
Match the method to the mixture: filtration, evaporation, distillation, separating funnel, chromatography, magnet.
Gas denser than air: downward delivery. Gas lighter than air: upward delivery. Gas not very soluble: over water.
Know the tests: hydrogen (squeaky pop), oxygen (relights glowing splint), carbon dioxide (limewater milky), ammonia (damp red litmus turns blue).
Graph: time on the x-axis, labelled axes with units, crosses for points, smooth curve of best fit. Always follow the safety rules.
